questions.q: A vernier callipers has 10 vernier divisions equal to 9 main-scale divisions, and one main-scale division is 1 mm. What is its least count?
questions.why: Least count = 1 MSD − 1 VSD = 1 mm − 0.9 mm = 0.1 mm, which is 0.01 cm.

questions.q: With the jaws of a vernier callipers closed, the vernier zero lies to the right of the main-scale zero. The zero error is
o: negative, and it is added to the reading
positive, and it is subtracted from the reading
positive, and it is added to the reading
negative, and it is subtracted from the reading
questions.why: A vernier zero to the right of the main-scale zero gives a positive error; the corrected reading is the observed reading minus the zero error.

questions.q: Roughly how long is a seconds pendulum on the Earth?
questions.why: A seconds pendulum has a period of 2 s; l = gT² ÷ 4π² = 9.8 × 4 ÷ 39.5 ≈ 0.99 m.

questions.q: A screw gauge has a pitch of 1 mm and 100 divisions on its circular scale. Its least count is
questions.why: Least count = pitch ÷ number of circular-scale divisions = 1 mm ÷ 100 = 0.01 mm.

questions.q: Which change does NOT alter the time period of a simple pendulum swinging through small angles?
o: Using a heavier bob of the same size
Taking the pendulum to the Moon
questions.why: T = 2π√(l/g) depends only on the effective length and g, not on the mass of the bob.

long.q: Define the least count of a vernier callipers and give its formula.
scheme: B1: the least count is the smallest length that the instrument can measure accurately
B1: least count = value of one main-scale division ÷ total number of divisions on the vernier scale

long.q: A vernier callipers of least count 0.01 cm has a zero error of −0.03 cm. While measuring the diameter of a cylinder, the main-scale reading is 3.2 cm and the 6th vernier division coincides with a main-scale mark. Calculate the corrected diameter.
scheme: C1: observed reading = 3.2 + 6 × 0.01 = 3.26 cm
M1: corrected reading = observed reading − zero error = 3.26 − (−0.03)
A1: diameter = 3.29 cm

long.q: A screw gauge has a pitch of 0.5 mm and 50 divisions on its circular scale. (a) Calculate its least count. (b) With no zero error, the main-scale reading for a wire is 4.5 mm and the 32nd circular division is on the reference line. Find the diameter of the wire.
scheme: C1: least count = pitch ÷ number of circular divisions = 0.5 ÷ 50
A1: least count = 0.01 mm
M1: diameter = main-scale reading + (circular division × least count) = 4.5 + 32 × 0.01
A1: diameter = 4.82 mm

long.q: A simple pendulum makes 20 complete oscillations in 40 s. (a) Find its time period and frequency. (b) Is it a seconds pendulum? Give a reason. (c) What will its time period be if its effective length is made four times as long?
scheme: C1: time period T = 40 ÷ 20 = 2 s
B1: frequency f = 1 ÷ T = 0.5 Hz
B1: yes, because a seconds pendulum has a time period of exactly 2 s
M1: T ∝ √l, so new T = 2 × √4
A1: new time period = 4 s

long.q: Give reasons: (a) the time for 20 oscillations is measured rather than for one oscillation; (b) the bob of a simple pendulum should be small and heavy; (c) the pendulum should be made to swing through a small angle.
scheme: B1: it reduces the effect of the reaction-time error in starting and stopping the stopwatch, so the period found is more accurate
B1: a small heavy bob behaves like a point mass and is least affected by air resistance, so it keeps swinging longer
B1: the relation T = 2π√(l/g) holds only for small amplitudes, so the period stays constant

questions.q: The slope of a velocity–time graph gives the
questions.why: Slope = change in velocity ÷ time taken, which is acceleration.

questions.q: The area under a velocity–time graph gives the
questions.why: Area = velocity × time, which is the displacement in that interval.

questions.q: A runner goes exactly once round a circular track of radius r and stops at the starting point. Her displacement is
questions.why: Displacement is the straight-line distance from the start to the finish; she ends where she began, so it is zero.

questions.q: A car moving at 20 m s⁻¹ is brought to rest uniformly in 5 s. Its retardation is
questions.why: Retardation = (20 − 0) ÷ 5 = 4 m s⁻².

questions.q: A stone is dropped from rest. Taking g = 10 m s⁻², its speed after 3 s is
questions.why: v = u + gt = 0 + 10 × 3 = 30 m s⁻¹. 45 m is the distance fallen, not the speed.

long.q: Give two differences between distance and displacement.
scheme: B1: distance is the total length of the path travelled and is a scalar
B1: displacement is the shortest straight-line distance from the initial to the final position in a stated direction; it is a vector and can be zero

long.q: A train starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 0.5 m s⁻² for 1 minute. Calculate (a) the speed it reaches, (b) the distance it covers in this time.
scheme: A1: v = 30 m s⁻¹
M1: s = ut + ½at² = 0 + ½ × 0.5 × 60²

long.q: A ball is thrown vertically upwards with a speed of 20 m s⁻¹. Taking g = 10 m s⁻² and ignoring air resistance, calculate (a) the maximum height reached, (b) the time taken to reach it.
scheme: M1: at the top v = 0, so 0 = 20² − 2 × 10 × h
A1: t = 2 s

long.q: Describe in words the shape of the velocity–time graph for a body (a) moving with uniform velocity, (b) starting from rest with uniform acceleration, (c) slowing down uniformly to rest.
scheme: B1: a straight line parallel to the time axis
B1: a straight line starting from the origin and sloping upwards
B1: a straight line sloping downwards that meets the time axis

long.q: A car starts from rest and its velocity increases uniformly to 12 m s⁻¹ in 4 s. It then moves at 12 m s⁻¹ for 6 s and finally slows uniformly to rest in 2 s. Calculate (a) the acceleration in the first 4 s, (b) the retardation in the last 2 s, (c) the total distance travelled, using the velocity–time graph.
scheme: C1: acceleration = 12 ÷ 4
A1: acceleration = 3 m s⁻²
B1: retardation = 12 ÷ 2 = 6 m s⁻²
M1: distance = area under the graph = ½ × 4 × 12 + 12 × 6 + ½ × 2 × 12
A1: distance = 24 + 72 + 12 = 108 m

questions.q: Passengers in a bus fall forward when the bus brakes suddenly. This is due to
questions.why: Their bodies tend to keep moving forward while the bus slows down: inertia of motion.

questions.q: The SI unit of linear momentum is
questions.why: Momentum = mass × velocity, so its unit is kg × m s⁻¹ (equivalent to N s).

questions.q: A force of 10 N acts on a body of mass 2 kg. Its acceleration is
If the distance between two bodies is doubled, the gravitational force between them becomes
questions.why: F ∝ 1/r², so doubling r makes the force 1/2² = 1/4 of its value.

questions.q: Which of these is a non-contact force?
questions.why: A magnet attracts iron from a distance without touching it; the others need contact.

long.q: State Newton's second law of motion and use it to show that F = ma.
scheme: B1: the rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the applied force and takes place in the direction of the force
M1: F ∝ (mv − mu) ÷ t = m(v − u) ÷ t
A1: since (v − u) ÷ t = a, F = kma, and with k = 1 in SI units F = ma

long.q: A cricket ball of mass 150 g moving at 20 m s⁻¹ is stopped by a fielder in 0.1 s. Calculate (a) the change in momentum of the ball, (b) the average force applied by the fielder. (c) Why does the fielder draw his hands back while catching?
scheme: C1: change in momentum = 0.15 × (0 − 20)
A1: magnitude = 3 kg m s⁻¹
C1: F = change in momentum ÷ time = 3 ÷ 0.1
B1: drawing the hands back increases the time taken to stop the ball, so the force on the hands is smaller

long.q: Give reasons: (a) a gun recoils when a bullet is fired; (b) a person can walk forward only by pushing the ground backwards; (c) dust comes out of a carpet when it is beaten with a stick.
scheme: B1: the gun pushes the bullet forward and, by Newton's third law, the bullet pushes the gun back with an equal and opposite force
B1: the foot pushes the ground backwards (action) and the ground pushes the foot forwards (reaction), which moves the person forward
B1: the carpet moves when struck but the dust particles tend to stay at rest due to inertia of rest, so they separate and fall out

long.q: An astronaut has a mass of 60 kg. Taking g on the Earth as 10 m s⁻² and on the Moon as one-sixth of that, find (a) his weight on the Earth, (b) his weight on the Moon, (c) his mass on the Moon, with a reason.
scheme: C1: weight on Earth W = mg = 60 × 10
B1: weight on Moon = 600 ÷ 6 = 100 N
B1: mass on the Moon is still 60 kg, because mass is the quantity of matter and does not depend on g

long.q: State Newton's law of gravitation, write it as an equation, and give the value of G with its SI unit.
scheme: B1: every body attracts every other body with a force directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them
B1: F = G m₁m₂ ÷ r²
B1: G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²

topics.name: Pressure in Fluids and Atmospheric Pressure

questions.q: The SI unit of pressure is the
questions.why: Pressure = thrust ÷ area, measured in N m⁻², which is called the pascal (Pa).

questions.q: Taking density of water = 1000 kg m⁻³ and g = 10 m s⁻², the pressure due to water alone at a depth of 10 m is
At sea level, the mercury column in a simple barometer stands at about
questions.why: Normal atmospheric pressure supports about 76 cm (760 mm) of mercury.

questions.q: A hydraulic press works on
questions.why: Pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted equally in all directions, so a small effort on a small piston lifts a large load on a big piston.

questions.q: A sudden fall in the reading of a barometer indicates that
questions.why: A sudden drop in air pressure is a sign of a storm; a gradual fall suggests rain.

long.q: Distinguish between thrust and pressure, giving the SI unit of each.
scheme: B1: thrust is the total force acting normally on a surface; its SI unit is the newton (N)
B1: pressure is the thrust per unit area; its SI unit is the pascal (N m⁻²)

long.q: Give reasons: (a) the wall of a dam is made thicker at the bottom; (b) wide wooden or concrete sleepers are placed under railway lines; (c) a sharp knife cuts more easily than a blunt one.
scheme: B1: liquid pressure increases with depth, so the bottom of the wall must withstand a greater pressure
B1: the sleepers spread the weight of the train over a larger area, reducing the pressure on the ground
B1: a sharp edge has a very small area, so the same force produces a much greater pressure

long.q: In a hydraulic press the small piston has an area of 10 cm² and the large piston an area of 500 cm². An effort of 40 N is applied to the small piston. Find (a) the pressure produced on the liquid, (b) the load that the large piston can lift.
scheme: A1: P = 4 × 10⁴ Pa
M1: by Pascal's law the same pressure acts on the large piston: load = 4 × 10⁴ × 500 × 10⁻⁴
A1: load = 2000 N

long.q: A tank is filled with water to a depth of 2.5 m. Taking the density of water as 1000 kg m⁻³, g = 10 m s⁻² and atmospheric pressure as 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa, find (a) the pressure due to the water at the bottom, (b) the total pressure at the bottom.
scheme: B1: total pressure = 1.0 × 10⁵ + 2.5 × 10⁴ = 1.25 × 10⁵ Pa

long.q: Describe in words how a simple mercury barometer is set up and what it shows. Give one reason why mercury is preferred to water, and calculate the height of a water barometer when the mercury barometer reads 76 cm (relative density of mercury = 13.6).
scheme: B1: a thick-walled glass tube about 1 m long, closed at one end, is completely filled with mercury
B1: the open end is closed with the thumb, the tube is inverted into a trough of mercury and the thumb is removed
B1: the mercury falls to about 76 cm above the level in the trough, leaving a vacuum at the top; this vertical height measures the atmospheric pressure
B1: mercury is very dense, so the column is short (it also does not wet glass and has low vapour pressure)
M1: height of water = 0.76 × 13.6
A1: about 10.3 m

topics.name: Upthrust in Fluids, Archimedes' Principle and Floatation

questions.q: The upthrust on a body that is completely immersed in a liquid depends on
o: its volume and the density of the liquid
the depth to which it is immersed
questions.why: Upthrust = volume displaced × density of liquid × g; when fully immersed, the volume displaced equals the body's volume.

questions.q: A body weighs 50 N in air and 30 N when fully immersed in water. The upthrust on it is
questions.why: Upthrust = apparent loss in weight = 50 − 30 = 20 N.

questions.q: The unit of relative density is
questions.why: Relative density is a ratio of two densities, so the units cancel.

questions.q: A block floats in water with two-fifths of its volume above the surface. Its density is (density of water = 1000 kg m⁻³)
questions.why: For a floating body, fraction submerged = its density ÷ density of water; 3/5 × 1000 = 600 kg m⁻³.

questions.q: A ship sails from a river into the sea. The ship
questions.why: Sea water is denser, so a smaller volume must be displaced to balance the same weight.

long.q: State Archimedes' principle.
scheme: B1: when a body is immersed wholly or partially in a fluid, it experiences an upthrust
B1: which is equal to the weight of the fluid displaced by it

long.q: A solid weighs 2.4 N in air, 1.6 N when fully immersed in water and 1.76 N when fully immersed in a liquid. Calculate (a) the relative density of the solid, (b) the relative density of the liquid.
scheme: C1: loss of weight in water = 2.4 − 1.6 = 0.8 N
A1: R.D. of solid = 2.4 ÷ 0.8 = 3
M1: R.D. of liquid = loss in liquid ÷ loss in water = (2.4 − 1.76) ÷ 0.8
A1: R.D. of liquid = 0.8

long.q: State the principle of floatation. Use it to explain why an iron nail sinks in water but a ship made of iron floats.
scheme: B1: a body floats when its weight equals the weight of the liquid it displaces
B1: the nail is denser than water, so even when fully immersed the weight of water it displaces is less than its own weight and it sinks
B1: the ship is hollow, so its average density is less than that of water and it displaces water equal to its weight before it is fully submerged

long.q: A wooden block measuring 20 cm × 10 cm × 5 cm has a density of 800 kg m⁻³ and floats in water (density 1000 kg m⁻³). Taking g = 10 m s⁻², find (a) the weight of the block, (b) the volume of the block below the water surface.
scheme: M1: floating, so upthrust = weight: V × 1000 × 10 = 8

long.q: Give reasons: (a) a balloon filled with hydrogen rises in air; (b) it is easier to float in sea water than in river water; (c) most of an iceberg lies below the surface of the sea.
scheme: B1: the weight of air displaced by the balloon is greater than the total weight of the balloon and gas, so the upthrust exceeds the weight
B1: sea water is denser, so it gives a greater upthrust for the same volume displaced
B1: ice is only slightly less dense than sea water, and the fraction submerged equals the ratio of their densities, about nine-tenths

questions.q: Water has its maximum density at
questions.why: Because of its anomalous expansion, water is densest at 4 °C.

questions.q: Heat is best described as
o: energy that flows because of a temperature difference
the degree of hotness of a body
a quantity read directly on a thermometer
questions.why: Heat is energy in transit, measured in joules; temperature is the degree of hotness.

questions.q: Which of these is a renewable source of energy?
questions.why: Wind is replenished naturally; the fossil fuels took millions of years to form.

questions.q: The main greenhouse gas released by burning fossil fuels is
questions.why: Burning coal, oil and gas releases carbon dioxide, which traps infrared radiation.

questions.q: In a food chain, roughly what fraction of the energy at one level passes on to the next level?
questions.why: About 10 % is passed on; the rest is used in life processes or lost as heat, so energy flow is one-way and decreasing.

long.q: Distinguish between heat and temperature, stating the SI unit of each.
scheme: B1: heat is a form of energy that flows from a hotter to a colder body; its SI unit is the joule
B1: temperature is the degree of hotness of a body, which decides the direction of heat flow; its SI unit is the kelvin

long.q: Describe in words how (a) the volume and (b) the density of a fixed mass of water change as it is heated from 0 °C to 10 °C.
scheme: B1: the volume decreases as the water is heated from 0 °C to 4 °C
B1: the volume is least at 4 °C and increases above 4 °C
B1: the density increases from 0 °C to 4 °C, reaching its maximum (about 1000 kg m⁻³) at 4 °C
B1: above 4 °C the density decreases

long.q: Explain how fish and other aquatic animals survive in a pond when its surface freezes in a cold winter.
scheme: B1: as the surface water cools to 4 °C it becomes denser and sinks, and warmer water rises, until all the water is at 4 °C
B1: below 4 °C the surface water expands, becomes lighter and stays on top, where it freezes at 0 °C
B1: ice is a poor conductor of heat, so it insulates the water below, which stays at about 4 °C and the animals survive

long.q: Explain the greenhouse effect, name two greenhouse gases and state one consequence of global warming.
scheme: B1: short-wavelength radiation from the Sun passes through the atmosphere and warms the Earth's surface
B1: the Earth emits long-wavelength infrared radiation, which is absorbed by greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane, trapping heat
B1: a consequence is the melting of glaciers and polar ice, which raises the sea level (any one valid consequence)

long.q: Give two differences between renewable and non-renewable sources of energy, with one example of each, and state two ways of reducing global warming.
scheme: B1: renewable sources are replenished by nature and will not run out, for example solar energy
B1: non-renewable sources cannot be replaced in a short time once used, for example coal
B1: use renewable sources such as solar and wind in place of fossil fuels
B1: plant more trees and use energy-efficient appliances and public transport

questions.q: A ray strikes a plane mirror with an angle of incidence of 35°. The angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray is
questions.why: Angle of reflection = 35°, so the angle between the two rays is 35° + 35° = 70°.

questions.q: How many images are formed by two plane mirrors inclined at 60° to each other?
A concave mirror has a radius of curvature of 30 cm. Its focal length is
questions.why: For a spherical mirror f = R ÷ 2 = 15 cm.

questions.q: The mirror used as a rear-view mirror in vehicles is a
questions.why: A convex mirror always gives an erect, diminished image and a wide field of view.

questions.q: A boy walks towards a plane mirror at 2 m s⁻¹. How fast does his image approach him?
questions.why: The image moves towards the mirror at 2 m s⁻¹ while the boy also moves at 2 m s⁻¹, so they approach each other at 4 m s⁻¹.

long.q: State the laws of reflection of light.
scheme: B1: the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection
B1: the incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane

long.q: State three characteristics of the image formed by a plane mirror.
scheme: B1: it is virtual and erect
B1: it is the same size as the object
B1: it is as far behind the mirror as the object is in front, and it is laterally inverted

long.q: An object is placed between the principal focus and the pole of a concave mirror. Describe in words how the image is located using two rays, and state its nature, position and size.
scheme: B1: a ray from the top of the object parallel to the principal axis reflects through the principal focus
B1: a ray from the top of the object travelling as if it came from the centre of curvature (along the normal) reflects back along itself
B1: the reflected rays diverge, so they are produced backwards and meet behind the mirror
B1: the image is virtual, erect, magnified and behind the mirror

long.q: Two plane mirrors are inclined to each other at an angle θ and form 7 images of an object placed between them. Calculate θ. How many images are formed if the mirrors are made parallel?
scheme: B1: parallel mirrors form an infinite number of images (in practice they grow fainter)

long.q: State one use each of a concave mirror and a convex mirror, giving a reason for each.
scheme: B1: concave mirror: a shaving or make-up mirror
B1: when the face is closer than the focus, the mirror forms an erect, magnified image
B1: convex mirror: a rear-view mirror in vehicles
B1: it always forms an erect, diminished image and gives a wide field of view

questions.q: Sound cannot travel through
questions.why: Sound is a mechanical wave and needs a material medium to travel.

questions.q: In a longitudinal wave, the particles of the medium vibrate
o: perpendicular to the direction of the wave
along the direction in which the wave travels
questions.why: Sound in air is longitudinal: particles vibrate back and forth along the wave's direction, forming compressions and rarefactions.

questions.q: A sound wave of frequency 500 Hz has a wavelength of 0.68 m. Its speed is
The audible range of frequency for a normal human ear is
questions.why: Below 20 Hz is infrasonic and above 20 kHz is ultrasonic.

questions.q: The speed of sound is greatest in
questions.why: Sound travels fastest in solids, then liquids, and slowest in gases.

long.q: Describe in words an experiment with an electric bell and a bell jar to show that sound needs a material medium to travel.
scheme: B1: an electric bell is hung inside a bell jar connected to a vacuum pump and is set ringing; the sound is heard clearly
B1: as the air is pumped out, the sound becomes fainter and is almost inaudible, although the hammer is still seen striking the gong
B1: so sound cannot travel through a vacuum; it needs a material medium

long.q: Give two differences between longitudinal and transverse waves, with one example of each.
scheme: B1: in a longitudinal wave the particles vibrate along the direction of propagation, forming compressions and rarefactions, e.g. sound in air
B1: in a transverse wave the particles vibrate perpendicular to the direction of propagation, forming crests and troughs, e.g. waves on a stretched string

long.q: A tuning fork of frequency 256 Hz produces sound in air, where the speed of sound is 320 m s⁻¹. Find (a) the wavelength, (b) the time period. (c) The sound then passes into water, where its speed is 1440 m s⁻¹. Find the new wavelength.
scheme: M1: the frequency does not change, so λ = 1440 ÷ 256
A1: λ = 5.625 m (about 5.6 m)

long.q: What are ultrasonic waves? State two uses of them.
scheme: B1: sound waves of frequency above 20 kHz, which humans cannot hear
B1: SONAR, to find the depth of the sea or locate submarines and shoals of fish
B1: medical scanning (ultrasonography) of internal organs, or cleaning delicate parts and detecting cracks in metals

long.q: Give reasons: (a) sound travels faster in humid air than in dry air; (b) sound travels faster in solids than in gases; (c) we see a flash of lightning before we hear the thunder.
scheme: B1: humid air is less dense than dry air at the same temperature and pressure, so sound travels faster in it
B1: solids are far more elastic than gases, so the vibrations are passed on more quickly
B1: light travels at about 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, far faster than sound (about 340 m s⁻¹ in air)

questions.q: The SI unit of electric charge is the
questions.why: Charge is measured in coulombs; 1 C = 1 A × 1 s.

questions.q: A charge of 30 C flows through a wire in 1 minute. The current is
An ammeter is connected
o: anywhere, since its resistance is high
questions.why: All the current must pass through the ammeter, so it goes in series; it has a very low resistance.

questions.q: In the external circuit, conventional current flows
o: from the negative to the positive terminal
in the same direction as the electrons
from the positive to the negative terminal
questions.why: Conventional current is taken from + to − outside the cell, opposite to the flow of electrons.

questions.q: Which of these is an insulator?
questions.why: Rubber has no free charges to carry a current; the others conduct.

long.q: Define electric current and state its SI unit.
scheme: B1: electric current is the rate of flow of charge, I = Q ÷ t
B1: the ampere, which is a flow of 1 coulomb per second

long.q: 60 J of work is done in moving a charge of 5 C between two points in a circuit. (a) Find the potential difference between the points. (b) If the current is 2 A, how long does it take for 5 C to pass?
The charge on an electron is 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Calculate (a) the number of electrons that make up 1 C of charge, (b) the number of electrons passing a point in a wire carrying 0.32 A for 10 s.
Describe in words a simple circuit you would set up to test whether a material is a conductor or an insulator, and how you would interpret the result.
scheme: B1: connect a cell, a key (switch) and a bulb in series, leaving a gap between two crocodile clips
B1: place the test material between the clips and close the key
B1: if the bulb glows the material is a conductor; if it does not glow it is an insulator
B1: for example, a copper wire makes the bulb glow but a plastic ruler does not

long.q: State three factors on which the resistance of a metal wire depends.
scheme: B1: it is directly proportional to the length of the wire
B1: it is inversely proportional to the area of cross-section of the wire
B1: it depends on the material of the wire and increases with temperature

questions.q: The best material for the core of an electromagnet is
questions.why: Soft iron is magnetised easily and loses its magnetism as soon as the current stops.

questions.q: Outside a bar magnet, the magnetic field lines go from the
o: north pole to the south pole
south pole to the north pole
questions.why: By convention the field lines leave the north pole and enter the south pole outside the magnet.

questions.q: Which statement about magnetic field lines is FALSE?
o: They are crowded where the field is strong
Outside the magnet they start from the south pole
questions.why: Outside a magnet they start at the north pole; the other three statements are true.

questions.q: The surest test to show that a steel bar is a magnet is
o: attraction with a piece of iron
questions.why: Attraction happens with any magnetic material, but repulsion happens only between like poles of two magnets.

questions.q: The strength of an electromagnet can be increased by
o: increasing the number of turns of the coil
questions.why: More turns (or more current) give a stronger magnetic field.

long.q: What is magnetic induction? Explain the statement 'induction precedes attraction'.
scheme: B1: magnetic induction is the process by which a magnetic substance becomes a magnet when placed near a magnet
B1: the near end of the iron first gets the opposite polarity by induction, and only then is it attracted, so induction comes before attraction

long.q: State three properties of magnetic field lines.
scheme: B1: they start from the north pole and end at the south pole outside the magnet, forming closed curves
B1: two field lines never intersect each other
B1: they are close together where the field is strong and far apart where it is weak

long.q: Describe in words how you would make an electromagnet, and state two factors on which its strength depends.
scheme: B1: wind many turns of insulated copper wire closely on a soft iron rod
B1: connect the ends of the coil to a cell through a key; when current flows the soft iron becomes a magnet
B1: its strength increases with the number of turns in the coil
B1: its strength increases with the current through the coil

long.q: Give two differences between a permanent magnet and an electromagnet, and state one use of an electromagnet.
scheme: B1: a permanent magnet keeps its magnetism, while an electromagnet is a magnet only while current flows
B1: the strength and polarity of an electromagnet can be changed by changing the current, but a permanent magnet's are fixed
B1: electromagnets are used in electric bells, or in cranes for lifting scrap iron (any one)

long.q: Why is soft iron used for an electromagnet while steel is used for a permanent magnet?
scheme: B1: soft iron is magnetised easily by a small current
B1: soft iron loses its magnetism as soon as the current is switched off
B1: steel is harder to magnetise but keeps its magnetism for a long time

questions.q: The SI unit of moment of force is
questions.why: Moment = force × perpendicular distance, so its unit is the newton metre.

questions.q: A force of 20 N is applied perpendicular to a door at 0.3 m from the hinges. The moment of the force is
questions.why: Moment = F × d = 20 × 0.3 = 6 N m.

questions.q: For a body in uniform circular motion, which quantity stays constant?
questions.why: The magnitude of velocity (speed) is constant, but its direction, and so the velocity and acceleration, keep changing.

questions.q: The centre of gravity of a uniform ring lies
o: at the top of the ring
at its centre, where there is no material
questions.why: By symmetry the centre of gravity is at the geometric centre, even though no material is there.

questions.q: A body is in equilibrium under several forces. This means
o: the resultant force and the resultant moment on it are both zero
there is a net clockwise moment on it
questions.why: Equilibrium needs zero resultant force and zero resultant moment; the body may be at rest or moving uniformly.

long.q: Define the moment of a force and state its SI unit.
scheme: B1: the moment of a force about a point is the product of the force and the perpendicular distance of its line of action from that point (the axis of rotation)
B1: its SI unit is the newton metre (N m)

long.q: Give reasons: (a) the handle of a door is fixed far from the hinges; (b) a spanner with a long handle is used to loosen a tight nut; (c) a car's steering wheel is turned using both hands on opposite sides.
scheme: B1: a larger perpendicular distance from the hinges gives a larger moment for the same force, so the door opens easily
B1: the long handle increases the perpendicular distance, so a smaller force produces the turning moment needed
B1: the two hands apply equal and opposite forces that form a couple, which turns the wheel without moving it sideways

long.q: A metre rule is balanced at its 50 cm mark. A mass of 40 g hangs at the 20 cm mark. Where must a 60 g mass be hung to balance the rule again?
scheme: M1: by the principle of moments, 40 × (50 − 20) = 60 × d
B1: so the 60 g mass hangs 20 cm on the other side, at the 70 cm mark

long.q: A uniform metre rule of mass 100 g balances on a knife-edge at the 40 cm mark when a mass m hangs from the 20 cm mark. State the principle used and find m.
scheme: B1: principle of moments: for a body in equilibrium, the sum of anticlockwise moments about the pivot equals the sum of clockwise moments
C1: the weight of the uniform rule acts at its centre, the 50 cm mark, 10 cm from the pivot; m is 20 cm from the pivot

long.q: A stone tied to a string is whirled in a horizontal circle at constant speed. (a) Explain why its motion is accelerated. (b) Name the force that keeps it moving in a circle and state its direction. (c) Distinguish between centripetal and centrifugal force.
scheme: B1: the direction of its velocity changes at every point even though the speed is constant
B1: a change in velocity means the motion is accelerated, the acceleration being directed towards the centre
B1: the centripetal force, provided here by the tension in the string, acts towards the centre of the circle
B1: centrifugal force is not a real force; it is an apparent force directed away from the centre, felt only by an observer moving with the body

questions.q: A coolie carries a load on his head and walks along a level road. The work he does against gravity on the load is
questions.why: The force (upwards) is perpendicular to the displacement (horizontal), so W = Fs cos 90° = 0.

questions.q: 1 kilowatt hour is equal to
If the speed of a body is doubled, its kinetic energy becomes
questions.why: KE = ½mv², so doubling v multiplies KE by 2² = 4.

questions.q: A pump lifts 50 kg of water through a height of 10 m in 5 s. Taking g = 10 m s⁻², its power is
A body falls freely from a height h. At height h/2, ignoring air resistance,
o: its potential and kinetic energies are equal
its total mechanical energy has halved
questions.why: Half the potential energy has changed to kinetic energy, and the total stays constant.

long.q: Define one joule of work and state its relation to the erg.
scheme: B1: one joule is the work done when a force of 1 N moves a body through 1 m in the direction of the force
B1: 1 J = 10⁷ erg

long.q: A box is pulled 4 m along a level floor by a rope that makes an angle of 60° with the horizontal. The tension in the rope is 50 N. Calculate the work done by the rope.
scheme: M1: W = F s cos θ

long.q: A ball of mass 0.2 kg is dropped from a height of 20 m. Taking g = 10 m s⁻² and ignoring air resistance, find (a) its potential energy at the top, (b) its kinetic energy and (c) its speed just before it reaches the ground.
scheme: A1: PE = 40 J
B1: by conservation of mechanical energy, KE just before reaching the ground = 40 J
A1: v = 20 m s⁻¹

long.q: Two bodies of masses 1 kg and 4 kg have equal kinetic energies. Find the ratio of their linear momenta.
scheme: B1: KE = p² ÷ 2m, so p = √(2m × KE)
A1: p₁ : p₂ = 1 : 2

long.q: State the energy changes that take place in: (a) a hydroelectric power station, (b) a loudspeaker, (c) photosynthesis in green leaves, (d) the burning of coal.
scheme: B1: potential energy of stored water → kinetic energy of falling water → electrical energy
B1: electrical energy → sound energy
B1: light energy → chemical energy
B1: chemical energy → heat and light energy

questions.q: In a class III lever,
o: the fulcrum is between the load and the effort
the load is between the fulcrum and the effort
the effort is between the fulcrum and the load
the effort and the load act at the same point
questions.why: In class III levers (e.g. fire tongs, forearm) the effort lies between the fulcrum and the load.

questions.q: A pair of scissors is a
questions.why: The rivet (fulcrum) lies between the effort at the handles and the load at the blades.

questions.q: The efficiency of an ideal machine is
questions.why: An ideal machine has no friction and weightless parts, so output work equals input work.

questions.q: The mechanical advantage of an ideal single fixed pulley is
questions.why: It only changes the direction of the effort, so effort = load and MA = 1.

questions.q: The mechanical advantage of a class II lever is always
questions.why: The load lies between the fulcrum and the effort, so the effort arm is always longer than the load arm.

long.q: Define mechanical advantage and velocity ratio of a machine.
scheme: B1: mechanical advantage = load ÷ effort
B1: velocity ratio = velocity of effort ÷ velocity of load (= distance moved by effort ÷ distance moved by load)

long.q: Show that for any machine, mechanical advantage = efficiency × velocity ratio.
scheme: B1: efficiency η = work output ÷ work input
M1: η = (L × d_L) ÷ (E × d_E)
A1: η = (L ÷ E) × (d_L ÷ d_E) = MA ÷ VR, so MA = η × VR

long.q: A block and tackle system has a velocity ratio of 5. It lifts a load of 400 N with an effort of 100 N. Find (a) its mechanical advantage, (b) its efficiency, (c) the distance the effort moves to raise the load by 2 m.
scheme: M1: η = MA ÷ VR = 4 ÷ 5
B1: effort distance = VR × load distance = 5 × 2 = 10 m

long.q: Name the class of lever and state where the fulcrum is in: (a) a wheelbarrow, (b) a pair of fire tongs, (c) a see-saw, (d) a bottle opener.
scheme: B1: class II; the fulcrum is the wheel at one end
B1: class III; the fulcrum is the hinged end of the tongs
B1: class I; the fulcrum is the central pivot
B1: class II; the fulcrum is the edge resting on the top of the cap

long.q: Describe in words how a single movable pulley is arranged and show that its velocity ratio is 2. Such a pulley lifts a load of 300 N with an effort of 200 N. Find its efficiency and give one reason why it is less than 100 %.
scheme: B1: the pulley hangs in a loop of string with one end tied to a fixed support; the effort is applied upwards at the free end and the load hangs from the axle
B1: when the load rises by d, both segments of the string shorten by d, so the effort moves 2d and VR = 2d ÷ d = 2
A1: efficiency = MA ÷ VR = 1.5 ÷ 2 = 75 %
B1: part of the effort is used to lift the pulley itself and to overcome friction

topics.name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

questions.q: When a ray of light passes obliquely from air into glass, it
questions.why: Light slows down in the optically denser glass and bends towards the normal.

questions.q: Glass has a refractive index of 1.5. Taking the speed of light in air as 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, its speed in glass is
Total internal reflection takes place when light travels from
o: a denser to a rarer medium with an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle
a rarer to a denser medium with an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle
a denser to a rarer medium with an angle of incidence less than the critical angle
any medium to any other at any angle
questions.why: Both conditions are needed: denser to rarer, and i greater than the critical angle.

questions.q: A coin lies at the bottom of a beaker of water 12 cm deep. The refractive index of water is 4/3. The coin appears to be at a depth of
questions.why: Apparent depth = real depth ÷ n = 12 ÷ (4/3) = 9 cm.

questions.q: The refractive index of a medium depends on
o: only the thickness of the slab
questions.why: Each colour travels at a different speed in a medium, so n is larger for violet than for red.

long.q: State the two laws of refraction of light.
scheme: B1: the incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane
B1: for a given pair of media and a given colour, sin i ÷ sin r is a constant (Snell's law), called the refractive index

long.q: Define the critical angle. Calculate the critical angle for glass of refractive index 1.5 in contact with air.
scheme: B1: the critical angle is the angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the angle of refraction in the rarer medium is 90°

long.q: A tank is filled with water to a depth of 20 cm. The refractive index of water is 4/3. Find (a) the apparent depth of the bottom, (b) how far the bottom appears to be raised.
scheme: M1: refractive index = real depth ÷ apparent depth
C1: apparent depth = 20 ÷ (4/3)
A1: apparent depth = 15 cm
B1: the bottom appears raised by 20 − 15 = 5 cm

long.q: Describe in words the path of a ray of light passing obliquely through a rectangular glass slab. Define lateral displacement and state two factors on which it depends.
scheme: B1: on entering the slab the ray bends towards the normal
B1: on leaving the slab it bends away from the normal, so the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray
B1: lateral displacement is the perpendicular distance between the incident ray produced and the emergent ray
B1: it increases with the thickness of the slab and with the angle of incidence (and with the refractive index)

long.q: A ray of light falls normally on one of the shorter faces of a right-angled isosceles glass prism (angles 90°, 45°, 45°). The critical angle of the glass is 42°. Describe in words what happens to the ray, name one instrument that uses such a prism, and give two reasons why a prism is better than a plane mirror for this purpose.
scheme: B1: the ray enters the first face normally, so it passes into the glass without bending
B1: it meets the hypotenuse face at an angle of incidence of 45°, which is greater than the critical angle of 42°
B1: so it is totally internally reflected and leaves the other short face turned through 90°
B1: such prisms are used in a periscope (or binoculars)
B1: total internal reflection reflects almost all the light, and there is no silvering to fade and no multiple images as with a thick mirror

questions.q: The power of a convex lens of focal length 25 cm is
questions.why: P = 1 ÷ f (in metres) = 1 ÷ 0.25 = +4 D; a convex lens has positive power.

questions.q: The image formed by a concave lens is always
o: real and of the same size
questions.why: A concave lens diverges light, giving a virtual, erect, diminished image between the lens and its focus.

questions.q: For a convex lens to act as a magnifying glass, the object should be placed
o: between F and the optical centre
questions.why: Only within the focal length does a convex lens form a virtual, erect, magnified image.

questions.q: An object is placed at 2F in front of a convex lens. The image is
o: at 2F on the other side, real, inverted and the same size
questions.why: With u = 2f, the lens formula gives v = 2f and magnification −1.

questions.q: A lens of power −2 D is a
o: convex lens of focal length 50 cm
concave lens of focal length 50 cm
concave lens of focal length 2 m
convex lens of focal length 2 m
questions.why: Negative power means a concave lens; f = 1 ÷ P = 1 ÷ 2 = 0.5 m = 50 cm.

long.q: Define the principal focus of (a) a convex lens, (b) a concave lens.
scheme: B1: convex lens: the point on the principal axis where rays parallel to the axis converge after refraction
B1: concave lens: the point on the principal axis from which rays parallel to the axis appear to diverge after refraction

long.q: An object 4 cm tall is placed 30 cm in front of a convex lens of focal length 20 cm. Find the position, nature and size of the image.
scheme: M1: lens formula 1/v − 1/u = 1/f with u = −30 cm and f = +20 cm
A1: v = +60 cm, on the other side of the lens
M1: magnification m = v ÷ u = 60 ÷ (−30) = −2
A1: the image is real, inverted and 8 cm tall
long.ans: 60 cm behind the lens; real, inverted, 8 cm

long.q: An object is placed 10 cm in front of a concave lens of focal length 15 cm. Find the position and nature of the image.
scheme: B1: the image is 6 cm from the lens on the same side as the object; it is virtual, erect and diminished (m = 0.6)
long.ans: 6 cm in front of the lens; virtual, erect, diminished

long.q: Describe in words how a convex lens is used as a simple magnifying glass, using two rays, and state how the magnification can be increased.
scheme: B1: the object is placed between the principal focus and the optical centre of the lens
B1: a ray parallel to the axis refracts through the focus on the other side, and a ray through the optical centre passes undeviated
B1: the refracted rays diverge and appear to come from a point on the same side as the object, giving a virtual, erect, magnified image
B1: using a lens of shorter focal length (greater power) gives a larger magnification

long.q: Give three ways of telling a convex lens from a concave lens without using any measuring instrument.
scheme: B1: by touch: a convex lens is thicker in the middle than at the edges; a concave lens is thinner in the middle
B1: a convex lens can form a real image of a distant window on a screen; a concave lens cannot
B1: held close to print, a convex lens makes the letters look bigger; a concave lens makes them look smaller

questions.q: Which colour of white light is deviated the most by a glass prism?
questions.why: Glass has its highest refractive index for violet, so violet bends the most.

questions.q: The radiation used in the remote control of a television set is
questions.why: Remote controls send coded pulses of infrared radiation.

questions.q: Which list is in order of increasing wavelength?
o: Gamma, X-rays, UV, visible, infrared, radio
Radio, infrared, visible, UV, X-rays, gamma
UV, gamma, visible, X-rays, infrared, radio
Visible, UV, infrared, gamma, X-rays, radio
questions.why: Gamma rays have the shortest wavelength and radio waves the longest.

questions.q: The sky looks blue because
o: air absorbs blue light the most
air molecules scatter blue light much more than red light
air scatters red light the most
questions.why: Scattering by small molecules is proportional to 1/λ⁴, so short-wavelength blue light is scattered most.

questions.q: Danger signals are red because red light
o: is scattered the least, so it can be seen from far away
questions.why: Red has the longest wavelength of visible light, so it is scattered least by air and fog.

long.q: What is meant by dispersion of light? State its cause.
scheme: B1: dispersion is the splitting of white light into its constituent colours when it passes through a prism
B1: it happens because the refractive index of glass is different for different colours (wavelengths), so each colour is deviated by a different amount

long.q: Name the radiation that is: (a) used to sterilise surgical instruments and kill germs, (b) used to detect fractures in bones, (c) given out by hot bodies and felt as heat.
scheme: B1: ultraviolet radiation
B1: X-rays
B1: infrared radiation

long.q: State two properties each of infrared and ultraviolet radiation.
scheme: B1: infrared: it has a strong heating effect on the bodies that absorb it
B1: infrared: it is scattered less than visible light, so it passes through haze and fog
B1: ultraviolet: it affects a photographic film and causes certain substances to fluoresce
B1: ultraviolet: it kills germs and is absorbed by ordinary glass but passes through quartz

long.q: Explain why (a) the Sun looks reddish at sunrise and sunset, (b) clouds look white.
scheme: B1: at sunrise and sunset, sunlight travels a much longer path through the atmosphere
B1: most of the shorter-wavelength blue light is scattered away, and the red light, scattered least, reaches the eye
B1: cloud droplets are large compared with the wavelength of light, so they scatter all colours nearly equally, and the mixture looks white

long.q: Describe in words how a spectrum of white light is obtained with a prism, state which colour is deviated least, give the approximate wavelength range of visible light and state how the intensity of scattered light depends on wavelength.
scheme: B1: a narrow beam of white light is passed through a glass prism and the emergent light falls on a white screen, giving a band of colours
B1: red is deviated least and violet most, with the order violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, red
B1: visible light has wavelengths from about 4000 Å (violet) to 8000 Å (red)
B1: the intensity of scattered light is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the wavelength (∝ 1/λ⁴)

questions.q: Taking the speed of sound in air as 340 m s⁻¹, the minimum distance from a reflector for a distinct echo is
questions.why: The echo must arrive at least 0.1 s later, so 2d = 340 × 0.1 and d = 17 m.

questions.q: The pitch of a sound depends on its
questions.why: A higher frequency gives a shriller (higher-pitched) sound.

questions.q: Soldiers are told to break step while marching across a bridge to avoid
questions.why: If the marching frequency matched the bridge's natural frequency, its vibrations could build up dangerously.

questions.q: A violin and a flute play notes of the same pitch and loudness. We can tell them apart by their
questions.why: Quality depends on the waveform, i.e. the overtones present with the main note.

questions.q: The unit used for the loudness level of sound is the
questions.why: Loudness level is measured on the decibel (dB) scale.

long.q: Distinguish between natural vibrations and forced vibrations.
scheme: B1: natural vibrations are the vibrations of a body at its own natural frequency when it is disturbed and left free to vibrate
B1: forced vibrations are the vibrations of a body under an external periodic force, at the frequency of that force

long.q: A boy standing 85 m from a cliff claps his hands and hears the echo 0.5 s later. Calculate the speed of sound in air.
scheme: B1: the sound travels to the cliff and back, a distance of 2 × 85 = 170 m
M1: speed = distance ÷ time = 170 ÷ 0.5
A1: speed = 340 m s⁻¹

long.q: A ship sends an ultrasonic pulse towards the sea bed and receives the echo 4 s later. The speed of sound in sea water is 1500 m s⁻¹. Calculate the depth of the sea and state why ultrasound is used rather than audible sound.
scheme: M1: depth = (speed × time) ÷ 2
A1: depth = 3000 m
B1: ultrasound has a very short wavelength, so it travels as a narrow beam without spreading and is reflected well by small objects

long.q: What is resonance? Describe in words a simple experiment to demonstrate it, and give one harmful and one useful example of resonance.
scheme: B1: resonance is a special case of forced vibration in which the frequency of the applied force equals the natural frequency of the body, so it vibrates with a large amplitude
B1: hold a vibrating tuning fork over a tube of air whose length is changed by raising or lowering the water in it; at one particular length a loud sound is heard
B1: harmful: a bridge may vibrate violently if marching soldiers keep step at its natural frequency
B1: useful: tuning a radio, where the circuit is set to resonate with the frequency of the wanted station

long.q: How does the loudness of a sound change if its amplitude is doubled? State two other factors on which loudness depends.
scheme: B1: loudness is proportional to the square of the amplitude, so it becomes four times as loud
B1: loudness increases with the surface area of the vibrating body
B1: loudness decreases as the distance from the source increases (and depends on the density of the medium)

questions.q: A 2 kW heater is used for 3 hours a day for 30 days. The electrical energy used is
questions.why: Energy = P × t = 2 kW × 3 h × 30 = 180 kWh.

long.q: State Ohm's law and describe the shape of the V–I graph for an ohmic conductor.
scheme: B1: the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across its ends, provided its temperature and other physical conditions stay the same
B1: the graph is a straight line passing through the origin; the slope of the V–I graph gives the resistance

long.q: A cell of e.m.f. 3 V and internal resistance 1 Ω is connected to two 4 Ω resistors joined in parallel. Find (a) the total current drawn from the cell, (b) the terminal voltage, (c) the current in each 4 Ω resistor.
scheme: C1: parallel resistance = (4 × 4) ÷ (4 + 4) = 2 Ω
A1: I = 1 A
B1: terminal voltage V = IR = 1 × 2 = 2 V
B1: the current divides equally, 0.5 A in each resistor

long.q: Distinguish between the e.m.f. and the terminal voltage of a cell. When are they equal?
scheme: B1: e.m.f. is the potential difference across the terminals when no current is drawn (the energy given to each coulomb by the cell)
B1: terminal voltage is the potential difference across the terminals when the cell supplies a current; it is less than the e.m.f. by Ir
B1: they are equal when the cell is in an open circuit (no current), or if its internal resistance were zero

long.q: A household uses five 60 W bulbs for 6 hours a day and a 1.5 kW geyser for 2 hours a day. Calculate the cost of electricity for 30 days at ₹7 per kWh.
scheme: C1: bulbs: 5 × 60 × 6 = 1800 Wh = 1.8 kWh per day
C1: geyser: 1.5 × 2 = 3.0 kWh per day
M1: energy in 30 days = (1.8 + 3.0) × 30 = 144 kWh

long.q: A wire of resistance 8 Ω is stretched uniformly until its length is doubled. Find its new resistance.
scheme: B1: the volume stays the same, so when the length doubles the area of cross-section is halved
M1: R = ρl ÷ A, so new R = ρ(2l) ÷ (A/2) = 4R
A1: new resistance = 32 Ω

questions.why: When the fuse in the live wire melts, the appliance is cut off from the high potential.

questions.q: A fuse wire is made of a material with
o: high resistance and low melting point
low resistance and high melting point
high resistance and high melting point
questions.why: It must heat up and melt quickly when the current exceeds its rating.

questions.q: According to the new international convention, the earth wire is coloured
questions.why: Live is brown, neutral light blue and earth green or green-yellow.

questions.q: The earth pin of a three-pin plug is made longer so that
o: it looks different from the other two
the appliance is earthed before the live connection is made
it fits only one type of socket
questions.why: The longer pin enters the socket first and leaves it last, so the metal body is always earthed while it is live.

questions.q: Which fuse is most suitable for a 1 kW electric iron on a 220 V supply?
questions.why: Normal current = 1000 ÷ 220 ≈ 4.5 A, so a 5 A fuse is just above it.

long.q: Why is a switch always connected in the live wire?
scheme: B1: when the switch is off, the appliance is disconnected from the live wire and is no longer at a high potential
B1: so it is safe to touch or repair; a switch in the neutral wire would leave the appliance live even when switched off

long.q: An electric kettle is rated 2.2 kW, 220 V. Calculate the current it draws and suggest a suitable fuse rating.
scheme: B1: a fuse rated slightly above 10 A, for example 12 A or 15 A, should be used

long.q: Describe in words the ring system of house wiring and give two advantages of it.
scheme: B1: the live, neutral and earth wires each run in a closed loop (ring) around the house, starting from and returning to the main fuse box
B1: each socket is connected to the ring through its own fuse
B1: current reaches each socket by two paths, so thinner wires can be used
B1: each appliance has its own fuse, so a fault affects only that appliance

long.q: What is earthing? Explain how it protects a person if the live wire accidentally touches the metal body of an appliance.
scheme: B1: earthing is connecting the metal body of an appliance to the earth through a thick wire of low resistance joined to a metal plate buried deep in the ground
B1: if the live wire touches the body, a large current flows to earth through this low-resistance path
B1: the large current blows the fuse (or trips the MCB), cutting off the supply
B1: the body stays at earth potential, so a person touching it does not get a shock

long.q: Describe in words how two two-way switches are used to control a staircase light from both the top and the bottom of the stairs.
scheme: B1: one two-way switch is fixed at the bottom and one at the top of the stairs, and the bulb is connected in series with them across the supply
B1: the two outer terminals of one switch are joined by two separate wires to the two outer terminals of the other
B1: changing the position of either switch completes or breaks the circuit, so the light can be switched on or off from either place

questions.why: Fleming's left-hand rule is used for motors; the right-hand rule is for generators.

o: more turns in the primary than in the secondary
more turns in the secondary than in the primary

questions.q: Lenz's law is a consequence of the law of conservation of
questions.why: The induced current opposes the change, so mechanical work must be done to produce electrical energy.

questions.why: Only a changing current gives the changing magnetic flux needed to induce an e.m.f. in the secondary.

scheme: B1: hold the wire in the right hand with the thumb pointing in the direction of the current
B1: the curled fingers then give the direction of the magnetic field lines, which are concentric circles around the wire

long.q: State Faraday's laws of electromagnetic induction and give one factor that increases the induced e.m.f.
scheme: B1: an e.m.f. is induced in a coil whenever the magnetic flux linked with it changes
B1: the magnitude of the induced e.m.f. is proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux
B1: it increases with the number of turns of the coil, the speed of the magnet or the strength of the magnet (any one)

long.q: State the principle of a d.c. motor and describe in words how it works, including the role of the split rings.
scheme: B1: principle: a current-carrying coil placed in a magnetic field experiences forces that produce a turning effect (Fleming's left-hand rule)
B1: a rectangular coil lies between the poles of a magnet and is connected to a battery through split rings and carbon brushes
B1: the forces on the two opposite sides of the coil are equal and opposite, forming a couple that rotates the coil
B1: the split rings reverse the direction of current in the coil every half rotation
B1: so the couple always acts in the same sense and the coil keeps rotating in one direction

long.q: A step-down transformer converts 220 V a.c. to 11 V. Its primary coil has 2000 turns. Find (a) the number of turns in the secondary, (b) the current in the primary when the secondary supplies 4 A, assuming the transformer is ideal.
scheme: M1: Ns ÷ Np = Vs ÷ Vp
M1: for an ideal transformer Vp Ip = Vs Is

long.q: Give three differences between an a.c. generator and a d.c. motor.
scheme: B1: a generator changes mechanical energy into electrical energy; a motor changes electrical energy into mechanical energy
B1: a generator works on electromagnetic induction; a motor works on the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field
B1: an a.c. generator uses slip rings; a d.c. motor uses split rings

questions.q: The SI unit of specific heat capacity is
questions.why: c = Q ÷ (mΔT), so its unit is J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹; J K⁻¹ is the unit of heat capacity.

o: has a higher specific heat capacity
gives out extra latent heat when it condenses
questions.why: Each gram of steam releases about 2260 J of latent heat on condensing before it cools like water.

questions.why: Water absorbs a lot of heat for a small rise in temperature.

long.q: Distinguish between heat capacity and specific heat capacity, giving the SI unit of each.
scheme: B1: heat capacity is the heat needed to raise the temperature of the whole body by 1 K; unit J K⁻¹
B1: specific heat capacity is the heat needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of the substance by 1 K; unit J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ (heat capacity = mass × specific heat capacity)

long.q: 200 g of water at 80 °C is mixed with 300 g of water at 30 °C. Assuming no heat is lost, find the final temperature of the mixture.
scheme: B1: heat lost by the hot water = heat gained by the cold water (principle of method of mixtures)

long.q: Calculate the heat needed to change 50 g of ice at 0 °C into water at 20 °C. Specific latent heat of fusion of ice = 336 J g⁻¹; specific heat capacity of water = 4.2 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹.
scheme: C1: heat to melt the ice = 50 × 336
C1: heat to warm the water = 50 × 4.2 × 20 = 4200 J
A1: total = 21 000 J

long.q: 40 g of ice at 0 °C is added to 200 g of water at 30 °C in a container of negligible heat capacity. Find the final temperature. Specific latent heat of fusion of ice = 336 J g⁻¹; specific heat capacity of water = 4.2 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹.
scheme: B1: check: cooling all the water to 0 °C would give 200 × 4.2 × 30 = 25 200 J, more than the 40 × 336 = 13 440 J needed to melt the ice, so all the ice melts
C1: heat gained by ice = 40 × 336 + 40 × 4.2 × T = 13 440 + 168T
C1: heat lost by water = 200 × 4.2 × (30 − T) = 25 200 − 840T

long.q: Describe in words the temperature–time graph obtained when ice at −10 °C is heated steadily until it becomes steam at 110 °C.
scheme: B1: the temperature rises to 0 °C and then stays constant while the ice melts (a flat part)
B1: it then rises steadily from 0 °C to 100 °C and stays constant at 100 °C while the water boils; this flat part is longer because the latent heat of vaporisation is much larger
B1: after all the water has boiled, the temperature of the steam rises again

questions.q: Which radiation is the most penetrating?
questions.why: Gamma rays need several centimetres of lead to stop them; alpha is stopped by paper.

questions.q: When a nucleus emits an alpha particle, its mass number decreases by
questions.why: An alpha particle is a helium nucleus with 2 protons and 2 neutrons, so A falls by 4 and Z by 2.

questions.q: A beta particle is
o: a fast-moving electron emitted from the nucleus
questions.why: It forms when a neutron in the nucleus changes into a proton and an electron.

questions.q: Isotopes of an element have the same
questions.why: Isotopes have equal numbers of protons but different numbers of neutrons.

questions.q: ²³⁸₉₂U emits one alpha particle and then one beta particle. The final nucleus is
questions.why: Alpha: A 238 → 234, Z 92 → 90. Beta: A unchanged, Z 90 → 91, giving ²³⁴₉₁Pa.

long.q: What is radioactivity? Is it affected by heating the substance? Give a reason.
scheme: B1: radioactivity is the spontaneous emission of alpha, beta or gamma radiation from the unstable nuclei of certain atoms
B1: no; it is a nuclear process, so it is not affected by physical conditions such as temperature or pressure

long.q: Compare alpha, beta and gamma radiations in terms of (a) charge, (b) penetrating power, (c) ionising power.
scheme: B1: charge: alpha +2e, beta −e, gamma no charge
B1: penetrating power: gamma > beta > alpha (alpha is stopped by paper, beta by a few mm of aluminium, gamma needs thick lead)
B1: ionising power: alpha > beta > gamma

long.q: A nucleus of radium ²²⁶₈₈Ra emits an alpha particle. (a) Find the mass number and atomic number of the new nucleus and write the equation. (b) What change takes place if this new nucleus then emits gamma radiation?
scheme: M1: alpha emission lowers the mass number by 4 and the atomic number by 2
A1: the new nucleus has A = 222 and Z = 86 (radon)
B1: ²²⁶₈₈Ra → ²²²₈₆Rn + ⁴₂He
B1: gamma emission changes neither A nor Z; the nucleus only loses energy

long.q: Distinguish between nuclear fission and nuclear fusion, giving one example of each.
scheme: B1: fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus into two lighter nuclei when struck by a slow neutron, releasing energy, e.g. uranium-235 in a nuclear reactor
B1: fusion is the joining of light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy, e.g. hydrogen nuclei forming helium in the Sun
B1: fusion needs extremely high temperatures (about 10⁷ K); in both, the energy comes from a loss of mass, E = mc²

long.q: State two uses of radioisotopes and two safety precautions while handling radioactive materials.
scheme: B1: in medicine, e.g. cobalt-60 to treat cancer
B1: as tracers, in carbon dating of fossils, or to sterilise medical equipment (any one)
B1: handle them with long tongs and store them in thick lead containers
B1: workers should wear lead-lined aprons and film badges, and not eat or drink near the sources
